procedural_history.originating_court: Assistant Director, Enforcement Directorate, Government of India, Hyderabad
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 02.03.2021 passed by the High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad in Criminal Petition No. 1148/2021
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Telangana at Hyderabad allowed Criminal Petition No. 1148/2021, granting anticipatory bail to respondent No. 1 in connection with F. No. ECIR/HYZO/36/2020 dated 15.12.2020, directing his release on bail in the event of his arrest for an offence under Section 4 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Directorate of Enforcement (ED) appealed to the Supreme Court, feeling aggrieved and dissatisfied with the High Court's judgment and order granting anticipatory bail to respondent No. 1. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the conditions stipulated in Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 are applicable to an application for anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

facts: An individual (respondent No. 1) was under investigation by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for the offence of money laundering under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
Apprehending arrest, the individual applied for anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) before the High Court.
The High Court granted anticipatory bail, ruling that the stringent conditions for bail under Section 45 of the PMLA were not applicable to anticipatory bail applications.
law: Section 45 of the PMLA imposes strict twin conditions for granting bail for a money laundering offence: the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
Section 438 of the CrPC provides the procedure for granting anticipatory bail.
The Supreme Court clarified the interpretation of its previous judgments in *Nikesh Tarachand Shah* and *Dr. V.C. Mohan*.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had misinterpreted the law by relying on the *Nikesh Tarachand Shah* case to conclude that Section 45 of the PMLA does not apply to anticipatory bail.
The Court pointed to its later decision in *Dr. V.C. Mohan*, which clarified that this interpretation was incorrect.

The Court held that while an application may be filed under Section 438 CrPC, if it is in connection with an offence under the PMLA, the "underlying principles and rigours of Section 45 must get triggered."
Therefore, the High Court was obligated to apply the strict conditions of Section 45 before considering the grant of anticipatory bail.
The Supreme Court also noted that the High Court failed to consider the seriousness of the economic offence on its merits, which is a crucial factor in such cases.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the stringent conditions for bail stipulated in Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002, are applicable to applications for anticipatory bail filed under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Consequently, it set aside the High Court's order granting anticipatory bail because it had failed to apply these mandatory conditions.

issue.issue_text: Whether the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the scheduled offence can be a ground to discontinue the investigation against an accused under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

facts: The respondent (accused No. 1) argued that the investigation against him under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA), 2002, should be discontinued.
The basis for this argument was that other co-accused in the underlying scheduled (or predicate) offence had already been acquitted or discharged.
law: The acquittal or discharge of co-accused in a scheduled offence is not, by itself, a sufficient ground to halt a PMLA investigation against another accused.
The crucial factor is whether an enquiry or investigation for the scheduled offence is still ongoing against the specific accused in question.
application: The Supreme Court noted that an enquiry and investigation were actively being conducted against respondent No. 1 in connection with the scheduled offence (FIR No. 12/2019).
The Court explicitly stated, "merely because other accused are acquitted, it cannot be a ground not to continue the investigation against respondent No. 1."

It reasoned that as long as an investigation into the scheduled offence is pending against an individual, the PMLA proceedings related to that offence can also continue against that same individual, regardless of the outcome for other co-accused.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the respondent's argument, holding that the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the scheduled offence is not a valid reason to discontinue the PMLA investigation against him, especially since an investigation for the scheduled offence was still ongoing against him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting anticipatory bail to the respondent for an offence under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.

facts: The respondent was under investigation by the Enforcement Directorate (ED) for the offence of money laundering under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA).
Apprehending arrest, the respondent applied for anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC).
The High Court granted anticipatory bail to the respondent, leading the ED to appeal this decision to the Supreme Court.
law: The strict conditions ('rigour') for granting bail laid out in Section 45 of the PMLA are applicable not only to regular bail but also to applications for anticipatory bail under Section 438 CrPC.

When dealing with serious economic offences like money laundering, which have a broad impact on society, courts must be very cautious and slow in exercising their discretion to grant anticipatory bail.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court made a fundamental legal error by holding that the provisions of Section 45 of the PMLA would not apply to an anticipatory bail application. The Supreme Court clarified that once an investigation is for an offense under the PMLA, the conditions of Section 45 are automatically triggered.
The Court also determined that, even on the merits of the case, the High Court's decision was flawed. The High Court failed to consider the serious nature of the money laundering allegations.
The Supreme Court observed that the High Court had treated the matter as if it were an 'ordinary offence under IPC' rather than a grave economic offense requiring thorough investigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, finding it 'erroneous and unsustainable.' The justification was twofold: first, the High Court incorrectly ignored the mandatory and strict bail conditions of Section 45 of the PMLA, which apply to anticipatory bail. Second, the High Court failed to properly appreciate the seriousness of the money laundering allegations, which, as a serious economic offense, warranted a much more cautious approach before granting pre-arrest bail.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The rigour of Section 45 of the Act, 2002 shall be applicable even with respect to an application for anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
obiter: The prospective overruling of a decision cannot be pressed into service to defend a judgment that was passed relying upon the law prevalent at that relevant time.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court erred in granting anticipatory bail because it failed to consider the seriousness of the alleged economic offences and did not apply the mandatory twin conditions for bail under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. The Court held that these stringent conditions are applicable to anticipatory bail applications under Section 438 of the Cr.PC, and that the acquittal or discharge of other co-accused in the scheduled offence is not a relevant ground to halt a PMLA investigation or grant bail to the accused.
legal_tests_applied: The twin conditions under Section 45 of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 are applicable to applications for anticipatory bail under Section 438 Cr.PC. This requires the court to be satisfied that: (i) the Public Prosecutor has been given an opportunity to oppose the application, and (ii) where opposed, there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty of such offence and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
In cases of economic offences that have a societal impact, the court must be very slow in exercising its discretion to grant anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Cr.PC.
policy_considerations: In case of economic offences, which are having an impact on the society, the Court must be very slow in exercising the discretion under Section 438 of Cr.PC.
